City Council Approves Riverfront Park Plan

By Maria Chen, staff writer

Published Tuesday at city hall

MARKER_NEWS_LEDE After three years of public hearings, redesigns, and two failed ballot measures, the city council voted 7-2 on Monday night to fund the first phase of the riverfront park redevelopment, clearing the way for construction to begin as early as next spring.

The approved plan covers the northern half of the disused rail yard between Fifth Street and the old granary, adding a promenade, a playground, a small amphitheater, and restored wetland along the bank. Phase one carries a price tag of $18.4 million, drawn from a parks bond voters approved last November together with a state land-and-water grant.

"This is the moment the riverfront stops being a rendering on a poster board," said Councilor Ana Reyes, who has championed the project since the first design charrette. "Families on the near north side have been promised a park for a generation. Tonight we finally funded it."

Opponents of the measure raised concerns about maintenance costs and the removal of 140 surface parking spaces used by warehouse workers. Councilor Dan Whitfield, one of the two no votes, argued the city should rebid the landscaping contract before committing the full amount.

"I support the park. I do not support writing a blank check," Whitfield said during the hour-long debate that preceded the vote.

City staff told the council that phase-one maintenance is estimated at $420,000 per year, to be split between the parks budget and a newly created riverfront improvement district. Property owners inside the district would see a modest assessment beginning in the second fiscal year of operation.

The design, by a local landscape architecture firm selected in 2024, preserves the granary's brick facade as the park's focal point and routes a new segment of the regional bike trail through the site. A planned kayak launch and fishing pier were moved into the second phase after engineers found the riverbank needed deeper reinforcement than early surveys showed.

Construction fencing is expected to go up once permits clear, which the city engineer estimated could happen within ninety days. The council also approved a companion measure requiring quarterly public reports on spending and schedule, a concession to critics who pointed at the overruns that hit the downtown library project.

Monday's vote drew the largest crowd the council chamber has seen this year. Supporters in green "Park Now" shirts filled two sections, while warehouse employees who would lose parking sat along the back wall. Public comment ran just over an hour, with speakers split roughly evenly between the two positions.

If construction stays on schedule, the city expects to open the promenade and playground in about eighteen months. Phase two, which still needs a funding source, would extend the park south to the ferry landing and add the kayak launch.
